title: Grace before meals
hookLine: nearly every tradition pauses before eating, each with its own words

lines: A PAUSE, ALL OVER THE WORLD.
cards: The plate lands. And then, in homes all over the world, there's a pause. Hands are held around a table in Ohio.
In a kitchen in Cairo, someone says a word under their breath. In Jerusalem, a hand rests on a loaf. In Tokyo, two palms come together.
In a Sikh temple in Amritsar, rows of people sit on the floor, side by side, as volunteers bring the food. Different words, different gods or none. The same pause.
The week of gratitude ends at the table.

teach.h: WHO BRINGS FORTH BREAD FROM THE EARTH.
teach.b: A few tables, each in its own words.
At a Jewish table, the blessing before bread thanks God who brings forth bread from the earth; there are other blessings for fruit, for wine, for other foods, and a longer grace after the meal.
At a Muslim table, many say bismillah, in the name of God, before the first bite, and alhamdulillah, praise belongs to God, at the end.
At many Christian tables, someone says grace, a short prayer of thanks, often with heads bowed; the English word grace comes from the Latin gratia, thanks.

Many Hindus offer food to God first, and receive it back as blessed food, prasad. In Zen monasteries, monks chant before eating, and one well-known chant reflects on how much work brought the food to the bowl.
In Japan, people of any faith or none say itadakimasu, roughly, I humbly receive.
And in the Sikh langar, the free kitchen, everyone eats the same meal, sitting at the same level, whoever they are.

Each of these means something particular to the people who say it, and many are addressed to God, so they don't blend into one. But look at what the pause itself does. It interrupts the rush from hunger to fork.
It reminds you that the food didn't come from nowhere: soil, rain, farmers, drivers, cashiers, the person who cooked. For a moment, a meal becomes an arrival, not a refill.

how: Observant Jews say a blessing before bread and a grace after meals; many Muslims say bismillah before eating; many Christians say grace; many Hindus offer food to God first; Zen monasteries chant before meals; in Japan people say itadakimasu; Sikh langar serves everyone the same meal side by side.

games.q: your plate lands in front of you and you're starving. what does the pause do before you eat?
o: reminds you how far the food came, and whose hands brought it.
games.why: the pause interrupts the rush from hunger to fork. for a moment, the meal is an arrival, not a refill.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, and trace it backward, a breath for each: the hands that cooked or packed it, who drove it, who stocked the shelf, who grew it, the rain and the soil.
If you pray, you can use your own tradition's words before you eat; if not, a silent breath and a thank-you to all those hands is enough.

wordCard.voice: Itadakimasu. Japanese for I humbly receive, said before eating: one of many pauses traditions take before a meal. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a blessing. Jewish tradition has a blessing before bread, fruit and wine, and a grace after meals.

carryVoice: Your line: the food arrived. The week in five lines: notice why it happened, blessings counted, thanks said, both true, and grace. And that's the week.
